svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. What the privacy label is, and what a study found when it was checked
svg.desc: On the left, how an application privacy label is produced: the developer declares the data collection themselves, the platform does not verify it, and the platform states in its own documentation that the developer is responsible for accuracy. On the right, the result when a research foundation examined forty of the most popular applications: nearly eighty percent of the labels were false or misleading, sixteen of the forty were graded poor, and only six were graded acceptable. A band below explains the exemption that permits much of this, under which data shared with service providers need not be declared. A closing band states what labels remain useful for despite this.
svg.text: Figure 2: The Label Is a Declaration, Not a Measurement
Standard guidance says the labels are self reported and "developers can lie". Somebody checked, and the number is worse than that phrasing suggests.

g.text: The developer fills in a form.
They declare what their application collects and shares.
Nobody checks it against the application.
There is no automated audit and no manual verification of
the declaration against what the binary actually does.
Its own documentation states that applications are
responsible for making complete and accurate declarations.
So the label is a claim by an interested party, published
unverified, in a standardised format that makes it look

svg.text: A research foundation examined the labels of 40 of the most
popular applications and compared them against the policies.

g.text: Among them a widely played game and two large social platforms.
Including a video platform, a maps application and a messenger.
Out of forty of the most downloaded applications in the store.

svg.text: The exemption that makes much of this technically truthful
Data shared with "service providers" does not have to be declared. The definition is narrow on paper and enormous in practice, so an application can transfer
a great deal of information about you to other companies and still declare that it shares nothing with third parties.
Two of the studied applications declared no third party sharing while their own policies described sharing with advertisers and platforms.
What the labels are still genuinely useful for

g.text: Comparing two applications that do the same job. Both declarations are unverified, but a large gap between them is still informative.
As a floor, never a ceiling. An application that admits to extensive collection is telling the truth about the minimum. One that admits to none has told you nothing.

svg.text: Treat a good label as an absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence, and check it against something the developer did not write.
Independent analysis of what an application actually contains is the check that is not self declared. Section 4 has the tools.
